report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: During the preparation of this work, the author used ChatGPT (OpenAI) to support translation, language editing, text condensation, and auxiliary verification of calculation and statistical-reporting procedures.
The author independently reviewed and verified all outputs, analyses, and interpretations, and takes full responsibility for the content of the manuscript.

The continuity hypothesis proposes that dream content derives from waking life, and numerous studies have shown that elements of recent experiences are incorporated into dreams (Hudachek & Wamsley, 2023; Palmieri et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The continuity hypothesis proposes that dream content derives from waking life, and numerous studies have shown that elements of recent experiences are incorporated into dreams <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Hudachek & Wamsley, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Palmieri et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, waking experiences are not uniformly represented in dreams.
A key question therefore concerns selection: which content gains access to dreams more readily than other content, and why?
Research has identified several factors that influence this selection.

These include the time elapsed since an experience (van Rijn et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?ag6VAo 2015) https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?3tNWpQ its personal and emotional significancehttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?McoqIO emotional intensity and novelty (Malinowski & Hortonhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?7slMGp 2014) , stress and experiences of threat (Baselgia & Rasch, 2026; Cartwright et al., 2006; Sikka et al., 2018) , relevance to current goals and concerns (Nikles et al., 1998) , the presence of unfinished goals or plans (Fechner et al., 2024) and the nature of the activity itself, such as social interactions (Schredl & Hofmann, 2003).
text.formatted: These include the time elapsed since an experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(van Rijn et al., 2015)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?ag6VAo">,</ref> its personal and emotional significance, emotional intensity and novelty <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Malinowski & Horton, 2014)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?3tNWpQ">,</ref> stress and experiences of threat <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Baselgia & Rasch, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Cartwright et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Sikka et al., 2018)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?McoqIO">,</ref> relevance to current goals and concerns <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Nikles et al., 1998)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?7slMGp">,</ref> the presence of unfinished goals or plans <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Fechner et al., 2024)</ref> and the nature of the activity itself, such as social interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Schredl & Hofmann, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Natural disasters meet several of these criteria and are therefore expected to be reflected in dreams.
The eruptions highlighted in the figure were not selected arbitrarily.
They include high-magnitude eruptions (VEI 5 -Hunga Tonga), as well as quiet, effusive, "tourist" eruptions associated with lava flows (VEI 0 -Fagradalsfjall, Iceland; Kīlauea, Hawaii).
The VEI scale ranges from 0 to 8 and is approximately logarithmic.
What these events have in common is not their magnitude but their media visibility, as confirmed by an independent review of coverage by major international news agencies and outlets (Leetaru, 2017).
text.formatted: What these events have in common is not their magnitude but their media visibility, as confirmed by an independent review of coverage by major international news agencies and outlets <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Leetaru, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: >Incorporation of Disaster-Related Content into Dreams
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Incorporation of Disaster-Related Content into Dreams</head>

text.text: The statistical analyses below show that the pattern observed in Figure 1 is neither an artifact of post hoc matching of events to the curve nor a phenomenon specific to volcanic eruptions.
text.formatted: The statistical analyses below show that the pattern observed in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> is neither an artifact of post hoc matching of events to the curve nor a phenomenon specific to volcanic eruptions.

text.text: >Method and Results
text.formatted: <head n="2.2." >Method and Results</head>

text.text: The primary measurement tool was Google Trends (GT), which enables the analysis of changes in search interest for specific queries across selected geographic areas and time periods.
The use of GT as a source of information on dream content has a precedent in the Google Trends project "The Shape of Dreams" (Fragapane, 2020).
text.formatted: The use of GT as a source of information on dream content has a precedent in the Google Trends project "The Shape of Dreams" <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Fragapane, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: One advantage of GT is that it enables the observation of spontaneous, natural behaviors directly related to specific dream content across large populations and over long periods.
In this sense, a search query and a dream diary entry share a similar observational status: both constitute a verbal trace of specific dream content.

GT, however, allows researchers to detect whether independently occurring external events (e.g., highly publicized volcanic eruptions) are accompanied by systematic changes in the frequency of dream-related queries.
For research questions formulated in this way, GT-based methodology is better suited than traditional approaches such as dream diaries.
Identifying individual characteristics of searchers or employing independent judges to code content is unnecessary.
What matters is simply whether, following a particular event, the frequency of verbal traces left by dreams increases.
GT does not report raw search volumes for a given phrase.
For a researcherdefined time period (e.g., 2012-2024, comprising 156 months) and geographic area (e.g., the Philippines), it draws a representative sample of all searches.
It then determines the proportion of this sample consisting of searches for the target phrase (e.g., "volcano dream meaning") in each of the 156 months.
This produces 156 values representing the ratio of target searches to all searches conducted in a given month.
The tool then scales this sequence of proportions to a 0-100 index over the specified period (here, 156 months).

A value of 100 indicates the month with the highest ratio of searches for the given phrase to all searches during the analyzed period, while the remaining values are proportionally lower (e.g., 50 indicates search interest half as high as that in the peak month).
A value of 0 indicates insufficient data for a given point, which may result either from an absence of searches or from search volume that is too low to be reflected by the tool (Google, n.d.).
text.formatted: A value of 0 indicates insufficient data for a given point, which may result either from an absence of searches or from search volume that is too low to be reflected by the tool <ref type="bibr">(Google, n.d.)</ref>.

text.text: When several phrases (e.g., "football" and "volcano") are analyzed within the same GT query, they are scaled jointly, and their values can therefore be compared directly.
Thus, a value of 90 for one phrase indicates relative search interest nine times as high as a value of 10 for another phrase.
For phrases with relatively high underlying search volumes, GT results are stable, and repeated sampling yields very similar time-series patterns.

Conversely, for queries with low underlying search volumes, GT samples are less stable, and repeated retrievals of the same series may return somewhat different values, with some observations taking a value of 0.
For this reason, in analyses sensitive to sampling variability (Hypotheses 2 and 4), each relevant query panel was retrieved 12 times, following the recommendations of Eichenauer et al. (2022).
text.formatted: For this reason, in analyses sensitive to sampling variability (Hypotheses 2 and 4), each relevant query panel was retrieved 12 times, following the recommendations of <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Eichenauer et al. (2022)</ref>.

text.text: For the same reason, in disaster analyses conducted at the regional or national level, where the more restrictive "X dream meaning" queries could yield sparse time series, broader "X dream" queries were used (e.g., "volcano dream," "earthquake dream," "tornado dream").
In worldwide analyses and all comparisons between disasters and sports, the more restrictive and unambiguous "X dream meaning" queries were employed.
This stricter approach was also necessary for sports comparisons, because phrases such as "football dream" or "boxing dream" may refer to aspirations or ambitions unrelated to sleep.
To avoid inconsistencies arising from cross-linguistic comparisons, English was used exclusively as the search language throughout the study.

The study analyzed "X" queries (e.g., "volcano," "football," "boxing") as behavioral indicators of users' attention to a given topic, whereas dream-related queries (e.g., "X dream meaning") were treated as population-level indicators of attention to the corresponding dream content.
An individual search need not arise from the user's own dream-it may concern another person's dream or stem from another source.

For analyses of temporal trends, however, what matters is the aggregate change in the frequency of such queries; an increase in this frequency was interpreted as a population-level indicator of an increased presence of the corresponding dream content.

We tested (1) whether the occurrence of a disaster was accompanied by an increase in search interest for that disaster, (2) whether the occurrence of a disaster was accompanied by an increase in searches for disaster-related dreams, and (3) whether an increase in search interest for a given disaster was accompanied by an increase in searches for such dreams.
Three types of disasters were selected for analysis: earthquakes, tornadoes, and volcanic eruptions.
These events were chosen because they typically have a clear, discrete onset and are difficult to predict far in advance, allowing for more precise observation of changes in search behavior.
Floods do not meet this criterion equally well as they may develop gradually.
Tsunamis were also excluded because their occurrence is often directly linked to earthquakes, which could result in partial overlap between the two event categories.
The method involved compiling a list of actual disasters and comparing the timing of these events with search patterns reflected in GT data.
Accordingly, three research hypotheses were formulated: H1.

The occurrence of an actual disaster will be accompanied by an increase in search interest in the corresponding phenomenon (e.g., a volcanic eruption will be accompanied by an increase in searches for "volcano").

The occurrence of an actual disaster will be accompanied by an increase in searches for disaster-related dreams (e.g., a volcanic eruption will be accompanied by an increase in searches for "volcano dream").

An increase in search interest in a particular type of disaster will be accompanied by an increase in searches for the meaning of dreams related to that disaster (e.g., "volcano" -"volcano dream meaning").
Hypothesis testing began by defining the analysis period as January 2012 through December 2024, comprising 156 consecutive months.
For a time series of this length, GT aggregates data at a monthly resolution.
Geographic units were then screened to identify areas affected by the analyzed disasters.

In the first step, the 249 geographic units included in the ISO 3166-1 standard (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?i31Grk.) were screened and those with populations of at least 10 million were selected.
text.formatted: In the first step, the 249 geographic units included in the ISO 3166-1 standard (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?i31Grk">International Organization for Standardization, n.d</ref>.) were screened and those with populations of at least 10 million were selected.

text.text: This criterion was intended to exclude countries that might yield insufficiently stable GT signal due to their small populations.
Each selected unit was then assessed to determine whether at least one of the analyzed types of disasters had occurred within it (see Supplement S01).
For each country meeting these criteria, the usability of the English-language GT time series for disaster-related dream queries was then assessed.
Based on pilot analyses, an arbitrary usability criterion was adopted: a series was considered usable if it contained at least eight months with values exceeding those of both adjacent months.
If a series did not meet this criterion, the corresponding country-disaster combination was excluded from further analyses due to potential signal instability arising from GT sampling variability.

At this stage of the screening, five countries met the criteria: the United States and India (for all three disaster types), the Philippines (for earthquakes and volcanic eruptions), and Canada and Australia (for tornadoes).

To mitigate the risk of local signals being diluted in geographically large countries, additional screening at a subnational level was conducted for the United States (9.83 million km²), India (3.29 million km²), Australia (7.69 million km²), and Canada (9.98 million km²); the Philippines (approximately 300,000 km²) was retained at the national level.
This subnational screening led to the exclusion of India and Australia because no usable GT signal was obtained at the subnational level.
Canada was also excluded because an independent, complete tornado registry covering the analyzed period was unavailable (see Supplement S01).
Ultimately, the United States and the Philippines qualified for the event-based analyses.
Within the United States, further narrowing of the analysis to the state level identified California (424,000 km²) for earthquakes and Texas (696,000 km²) for tornadoes.
The full geographic screening procedure is detailed in Supplement S01.
>Results

text.text: Hypothesis H1 predicted that the occurrence of an actual disaster would be accompanied by an increase in search interest for the corresponding phenomenon.

Event dates and parameters were obtained from independent catalogs: the Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program (Global Volcanism Program, 2025) for volcanic eruptions, USGS ComCat (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?SFQwq3) for earthquakes, and NOAA/NCEI Storm Events (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?s8Ha19.) for tornadoes.

text.text: GT time series for general queries about each disaster (e.g., "volcano," "earthquake," "tornado") were then retrieved for the selected geographic areas, and their values were examined to determine whether they were elevated during event months.
The significance of the observed increases was assessed using a seasonalitypreserving one-sided permutation test.
The mean GT value across event months was calculated to serve as the observed mean.

In each permutation, every actual event month was replaced with a randomly selected corresponding calendar month from the full pool of such months in the analyzed period (e.g., an actual May was replaced with a randomly selected May from 2012-2024), with months sampled without replacement.
Preserving seasonality (by matching calendar months) was important for tornadoes due to their seasonal occurrence.

This constraint was nevertheless applied to earthquakes and volcanic eruptions as well, thereby imposing a more restrictive-and thus more conservative-test of the hypothesis than unrestricted sampling from all months.
For each permutation, the mean GT value was recalculated.

The observed mean was compared against a null distribution of 1,000,000 randomly generated means; the p value was calculated as the proportion of permutations yielding a mean equal to or greater than the observed mean (see Supplement S04).

text.text: Across all three analyzed disaster types, actual events were therefore accompanied by significant increases in search interest for the corresponding phenomena.
These results supported H1.
Actual disasters were associated with measurable changes in search behavior.

Importantly, the analyses were conducted at the population level: GT indicators reflected the search behavior of users across the entire analyzed geographic area, rather than only that of direct witnesses to the event.
This means that for a substantial proportion of the population, exposure to the disaster was indirect, likely occurring primarily through media coverage.

text.text: In all four analyzed cases, mean search interest in disaster-related dreams was higher during actual event months than expected under the seasonality-preserving null distributions.

The effect was statistically significant for earthquakes in California, tornadoes in Texas, and earthquakes in the Philippines; for volcanic eruptions in the Philippines, it was in the predicted direction but did not reach statistical significance.

For volcanic eruptions in the Philippines, an additional analysis was conducted on the subset of nine events for which search interest in the general "volcano" query in the eruption month exceeded the mean value of that series across the entire analyzed period.
Within this subset, the increase in "volcano dream" searches was statistically significant, p = .016.

This finding suggests that the weaker effect in the full sample of 19 eruptions may reflect the inclusion of events that were noticed primarily by local observers and did not attract broader attention.

text.text: The results indicate that actual disasters leave a measurable trace in searches for disaster-related dreams.
In parallel, the association between worldwide search interest in each disaster type and searches for disaster-related dreams was tested.

For each disaster type, the full 156-month time series was used, and Pearson's correlation was calculated between search interest in the phenomenon itself (e.g., "earthquake") and search interest in dreams about that phenomenon (e.g., "earthquake dream meaning").

Because of autocorrelation in the monthly time series, p values were calculated using Newey-West standard errors robust to heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation, with a maximum lag of 12 months (HAC[12]).
text.formatted: Because of autocorrelation in the monthly time series, p values were calculated using Newey-West standard errors robust to heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation, with a maximum lag of 12 months <ref type="bibr">(HAC[12]</ref>).

text.text: Positive and significant associations were found for all three disaster types: volcanic eruptions, r = .297, p = .001; earthquakes, r = .300, p = .002; and tornadoes, r = .295, p = .013.
Thus, increases in general search interest in a given phenomenon were accompanied by increases in searches for corresponding dream content.
These results supported H3.
All raw data, corresponding calculations, and detailed results are provided in Supplement S02.
The results indicate that people respond to natural disasters with increased searches for disaster-related dreams.
The first indication of this association emerged in the U.S. "volcano dream" search series.
This finding was subsequently supported by several distinct statistical analyses involving different disaster types, conducted both locally and worldwide.

Associations were found between the occurrence of actual disasters and increases in searches for these dreams, as well as correlations between search interest in disasters and searches for such dreams.
Thus, despite relying on different measures and levels of analysis, all analyses converged on the same conclusion: natural disasters are clearly associated with searches for disaster-related dreams.
The analyses also serve to validate the measurement procedure used in this study.
Across all analyses, associations were observed in the expected direction, indicating that both the measurement tool and the procedure are sensitive to the phenomena under investigation.
The observed pattern of results is consistent with both the general continuity hypothesis discussed above and Threat Simulation Theory (TST; Revonsuo, 2000; Valli & Revonsuo, 2009).
text.formatted: The observed pattern of results is consistent with both the general continuity hypothesis discussed above and Threat Simulation Theory (TST; <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Revonsuo, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Valli & Revonsuo, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: TST posits that experiencing real threats during waking activates the threat simulation system (TSS).
During sleep, this system generates perceptually and behaviorally realistic simulations of threatening situations.
The repeated rehearsal of these simulations is theorized to have enhanced the ability to recognize, avoid, and cope with threats in the ancestral environment (Revonsuo, 2000; Valli & Revonsuo, 2009).
text.formatted: The repeated rehearsal of these simulations is theorized to have enhanced the ability to recognize, avoid, and cope with threats in the ancestral environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Revonsuo, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Valli & Revonsuo, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: According to TST, dreaming is not a random or accidental reflection of waking experience, but a selective process in which threat-related content receives particular priority.

Experiencing real threats during waking is hypothesized to increase TSS activity, and the intensity of the resulting dream simulations should be directly related to the degree of personal threat experienced in the original situation (Valli & Revonsuo, 2009).
text.formatted: Experiencing real threats during waking is hypothesized to increase TSS activity, and the intensity of the resulting dream simulations should be directly related to the degree of personal threat experienced in the original situation <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Valli & Revonsuo, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, the content of threat simulations may also derive from events learned about through the media: "These types of threats usually come to our knowledge through the mass media, and include elements such as exotic animals, war, floods and other natural catastrophes" (Valli & Revonsuo, 2009, p. 25).
text.formatted: Furthermore, the content of threat simulations may also derive from events learned about through the media: "These types of threats usually come to our knowledge through the mass media, and include elements such as exotic animals, war, floods and other natural catastrophes" <ref type="bibr">(Valli & Revonsuo, 2009, p. 25)</ref>.

text.text: Subsequent research suggests that the presence of threats in dreams is associated with both threats and stress levels experienced during the preceding day (Lafrenière et al., 2018).

text.text: The present findings concerning natural disasters are consistent with these predictions: disasters constitute threatening events, and their occurrence was accompanied by an increase in search queries referring to dreams about the same type of event.
Sporting events meet nearly all of the conditions considered conducive to the incorporation of waking-life content into dreams.
Moreover, in many respects, they satisfy these conditions far more strongly than natural disasters do.
Major tournaments and competitions, as well as individual matches, capture attention for many days.
Interest in sports is active, personal, and intentional: fans actively seek out information, anticipate the event, follow results, and repeatedly return to related content.
Engagement is strong and personal-people invest time and money, travel long distances, form fan clubs, get team names tattooed, and build part of their identity around their teams.
Sports evoke strong emotions, both positive and negative.
The outcome of a competition remains unresolved for an extended period, and event-related content is repeatedly thought about and revisited.
Sports-related content appears on bags of chips, in television advertisements, in public debates, and in statements by politicians.
Exposure to it is simultaneously intense, direct, voluntary, prolonged, and linked to personal goals.

By contrast, the average person encounters natural disasters only incidentallytypically briefly and "in passing"-unintentionally, and without personal involvement or direct experience, with their attention drawn to them involuntarily.
TST predictions.

The classification of threats employed in TST research is not limited to physical threats, but also encompasses threats to psychological well-being, subjectively experienced threats, and failures (Valli & Revonsuo, 2009).
text.formatted: The classification of threats employed in TST research is not limited to physical threats, but also encompasses threats to psychological well-being, subjectively experienced threats, and failures <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Valli & Revonsuo, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Natural disasters and sporting events therefore both fall within this classification, although they differ markedly in the strength and nature of the observer's personal involvement.

Given these differences, one specific TST prediction becomes particularly relevant: "only real threatening events can fully activate the threat simulation system" (Valli & Revonsuo, 2009, p. 18), and the intensity of subsequent dream simulations should be directly related to the degree of personal threat experienced in the original situation (Valli & Revonsuo, 2009, p. 19).

text.text: Based on TST's assumptions, sporting events should therefore provide a much stronger stimulus for generating intense threat simulations during sleep than brief media reports of disasters that remain both physically and psychologically remote.
Consequently, both the continuity hypothesis and TST raise the same question: how much more strongly are sporting events incorporated into dreams than natural disasters?
The analysis examined the extent to which search interest in sports was reflected in search interest in sports-related dreams.
Three sports were first selected to preserve symmetry with the three disaster types analyzed.
Football was chosen as a widely followed sport with global reach, for which interest is not concentrated primarily in any single country or region.
Basketball was included as a second team sport to assess whether any pattern observed for football was specific to that sport.

Boxing, by contrast, was selected as a qualitatively different sport-an individual sport based on direct physical competition, with a different event structure, symbolism, and mode of audience engagement.
This selection made it possible to assess whether the observed effect applied to sports as a broader class of content rather than to the specific characteristics of a single discipline.

Worldwide GT series were then used to compare the ratio of search interest in disaster-related topics to search interest in sports-related topics (volcano + earthquake + tornado relative to football + basketball + boxing) with the corresponding ratio for dream-related searches (volcano dream meaning + earthquake dream meaning + tornado dream meaning relative to football dream meaning + basketball dream meaning + boxing dream meaning).

The RR index (ratio-of-ratios) is algebraically equivalent to directly comparing the ratio of disaster-related dream searches to disaster searches with the ratio of sports-related dream searches to sports searches.
Because both ratios were calculated within separately normalized panels, the separate scaling of the panels does not affect the RR value.
This comparison yields two clear predictions.

text.text: In ordinary searches, sports-related content overwhelmingly dominated disasterrelated content, accounting for 91.4% of the combined representation of the six analyzed topics, whereas disaster-related content accounted for only 8.6%.
In dream-related searches, this pattern was reversed: sports-related content accounted for 31.1%, whereas disaster-related content accounted for 68.9%.
The ratio of disaster to sports representation was 0.094 in ordinary searches and 2.218 in dream-related searches.
The ratio of these two proportions was RR = 23.64.

This means that disaster-related content was represented in dream-related searches about 24 times more strongly than would be expected based on its representation relative to sports in ordinary searches.

In addition, this effect was present in each of the 13 analyzed years (13/13; exact one-sided sign test, p < .001); annual RR values ranged from 13.49 to 106.70, Mdn = 26.70 (all raw data and calculations are provided in Supplement S02).

Even the smallest advantage-between volcanoes and basketball-was RR = 8.67.

text.text: The result was contrary to the predictions derived from both the continuity hypothesis and TST.
The dwarf cast a larger shadow than the giant.
Two aspects are particularly striking: the reversal of proportions and the magnitude of that reversal.
Disaster-related content, despite being far less prominent than sportsrelated content in ordinary searches, strongly predominated in dream-related searches.
The contrast was substantial: the relative representation of disasters was approximately 24 times greater.
Thus, the factors identified by the continuity hypothesis as important for dreamcontent selection led to in incorrect predictions.
A potential source of bias should also be noted.
GT may underestimate conscious attention directed toward sports because a substantial proportion of sports-related engagement occurs outside search engines.
If so, the observed advantage of sports over disasters in ordinary searches is itself underestimated, meaning that the true magnitude of the anomaly may be even greater.

Why is content that satisfies the standard conditions for transfer to a lesser extenta media-reported disaster-more strongly represented in dreams than content that satisfies them far better-a sporting event?
Perhaps people do not have sports-related dreams, or experience them only very rarely?
Research indicates that sports-related dreams occur regularly among a broad range of people (Bulkeley & Schredl, 2024; Erlacher & Schredl, 2010).
text.formatted: Research indicates that sports-related dreams occur regularly among a broad range of people <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bulkeley & Schredl, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Erlacher & Schredl, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The present study likewise demonstrates that people regularly enter queries such as "football dream meaning" and "basketball dream meaning" into search engines.
The simplest possibility-that the low representation of sports-related dreams in searches reflects the fact that people simply do not dream about sports-can therefore be rejected.
People do dream about sports.
Perhaps sports-related dreams have some particular property that prevents them from responding to daytime events?
An additional analysis of the dynamics of all six topics was conducted to determine whether sporting events are reflected at all in dream-related searches.
Searches related to football and basketball dreams fluctuated in parallel with changes in search interest in the sports themselves.
The boxing series was too sparse to yield a reliable result.
Sports-related dreams are not "unresponsive."

Therefore, the large disparity in the relative representation of disaster-related and sports-related content in dream-related queries cannot be explained by a lack of responsiveness of sports-related dreams to sporting events.
Such a response does occur.
Nevertheless, sports-related content remains far less strongly represented in dream-related searches relative to the intensity of waking attention it commands.
Details of the analysis are provided in Supplement S07.
Perhaps, then, sports-related dreams occur frequently but are simply not "mysterious" enough to require interpretation?
"People may experience many sports-related dreams, but they consider them self-evident and therefore do not search for their meaning.
Hence the disparity in the observed searches."
An explanation based on the alleged obviousness of sports-related dreams raises further questions.
What is the empirical basis for claiming that sports-related dreams are "obvious"?
There is no scientific evidence to suggest that sports-related dreams are any less or more "mysterious" than dreams about animals, bodily injuries, disasters, or anything else.
If their alleged "obviousness" were supposed to stem from linking the dream to a recently watched match ("I dreamed about sports because I watched a match.
Obviously."), the same logic should apply to disaster-related dreams ("I saw a volcanic eruption on the news, so I dreamed about a volcano.
Obviously.").
There is no inherent reason why a sports-related dream should not contain ambiguous, unexpected, absurd, or symbolic elements.
"That boxer looked like my father!
Why couldn't I move before taking the penalty kick?"

Reasoning based on the alleged "obviousness" of sports-related dreams therefore has the structure of a classic just-so story: a known result is retrofitted with an explanation that could just as easily have been constructed for the opposite result-by invoking the ambiguous symbolism of athletic competition and the "simple obviousness of a smoking mountain" (Gould & Lewontin, 1979).

text.text: The alleged obviousness fails to explain the observed disparity.
The data suggest the existence of an underappreciated or previously unrecognized mechanism governing dream content selection.
Such a mechanism is posited by Phantom Anxiety Theory (PAT), described in greater detail elsewhere (Florkowski, 2026c).
text.formatted: Such a mechanism is posited by Phantom Anxiety Theory (PAT), described in greater detail elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Florkowski, 2026c)</ref>.

text.text: The present study was designed as a test of this mechanism.

The theory distinguishes between two operating modes of the human anxiety system: a reactive mode, triggered by a consciously or unconsciously identified threat and extensively described in the existing literature, and an endogenous mode, which generates a state of anxious readiness independent of the immediate presence of a threat.
Endogenous anxious arousal resembles the vigilance observed in animals whose survival depends on anticipating danger (Creel et al., 2014; Liley & Creel, 2008).
text.formatted: Endogenous anxious arousal resembles the vigilance observed in animals whose survival depends on anticipating danger <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Creel et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Liley & Creel, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: PAT proposes that, over millions of years, persistent exposure to lethal threats shaped the nervous systems of our ancestors, fundamentally embedding anxiety-based vigilance within them.
Such undirected vigilance is adaptive in an environment saturated with lethal threats.

However, in an environment largely devoid of ancestral existential threats, its evolutionary mismatch becomes apparent: anxious arousal continues to be generated despite the absence of corresponding threat objects.
This arousal is referred to here as phantom anxiety, by analogy to phantom pain (Ramachandran & Hirstein, 1998).
text.formatted: This arousal is referred to here as phantom anxiety, by analogy to phantom pain <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Ramachandran & Hirstein, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: Undirected alarm arousal is an unstable state because it strongly motivates the anticipation of potential threats; therefore, it is rapidly bound to any object capable of serving as an anxiety carrier.

This endogenous alarm is not a passive state of arousal: it initiates active environmental scanning, preferential detection of information signaling potential threats, and the prioritization of such information.

When suitable anxiety carriers are absent from the perceptual field, they may even be generated ex nihilo, as observed in a specific class of nightmares-generative nightmares (Florkowski, 2026b https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?cg85E4.
text.formatted: When suitable anxiety carriers are absent from the perceptual field, they may even be generated ex nihilo, as observed in a specific class of nightmares-generative nightmares <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Florkowski, 2026b</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?cg85E4">)</ref>.

text.text: An anxiety carrier, however, must be sufficiently credible as a threat.

An implausible object will quickly be recognized as fictitious and lose its regulatory function-such as the notion of evil Reptilians ruling the world-prompting the anxiety system to seek a more stable object.

The optimal anxiety carriers in a world largely devoid of immediate dangers are "safe threats" (Florkowski, 2026a)-objects sufficiently credible to provide a plausible justification for the underlying anxious arousal.
text.formatted: The optimal anxiety carriers in a world largely devoid of immediate dangers are "safe threats" <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Florkowski, 2026a)</ref>-objects sufficiently credible to provide a plausible justification for the underlying anxious arousal.

text.text: Distant natural disasters possess the properties of "safe threats," whereas sporting events do not.
The latter may generate concerns about goal attainment, but they do not evoke concerns regarding personal safety.
PAT therefore predicts that the endogenous mode of the anxiety system will assign special weight to disaster-related events, but not to sporting events.

The theory further assumes that sleep does not deactivate the selective vigilance of the anxiety system, because otherwise the system could not fulfill its alarm function: a sleeping mother is not awakened by a car passing outside the window, yet the quiet cry of her own child awakens her.

During the day, a sporting event may capture conscious attention many times more strongly, but after sleep onset, many of the processes that confer significance on it cease to organize ongoing mental activity.
The endogenous anxiety system, by contrast, remains active, and so do the contents to which it has previously assigned weight as potential threat objects.
To put it figuratively: if trumpeter A plays ten times louder than trumpeter B, while both are playing, we hear mainly A. But when A falls asleep, we hear B.

PAT therefore predicts that natural disasters should be disproportionately represented in dreams relative to sporting events, beyond what would be expected based on their relative share of waking attention.
The proposed mechanism generates additional predictions.
If a disaster enters dreams because it serves as an effective carrier of phantom anxiety, its impact need not depend on posing an actual threat to the dreamer.
Rather, the distance from the disaster may even facilitate its function as a "safe threat."
Two further hypotheses were therefore formulated:
Disasters occurring thousands of kilometers from the observer and posing no direct threat to them leave a trace in searches for corresponding disaster-related dreams.
Visually dramatic disasters that cause no damage, or only minimal damage, also leave a trace in searches for corresponding disaster-related dreams.

H4 was tested using search data from the United Kingdom, where English is widely spoken, residents experience only weak earthquakes that pose no direct threat, and volcanic eruptions do not occur; the disasters analyzed here occurred thousands of kilometers from the United Kingdom.
The analysis employed the queries "volcano dream" and "earthquake dream."
For both series, mean values from 12 independent GT retrievals were used (Eichenauer et al., 2022).

To maintain symmetry with the sample of 15 eruptions, the earthquake set comprised the 15 highest local peaks in worldwide GT interest in earthquakes.
The mean value for "earthquake dream" was 34.31, compared to an expected value of 19.86 (p = .005; see Supplement S06).

text.text: The results were therefore consistent with H4 for both disaster types, with the effect reaching statistical significance for earthquakes.
H5 was tested using worldwide data.

Of the 15 globally visible eruptive episodes previously identified based on worldwide peaks in GT interest in volcanic eruptions, all events meeting the adopted criterion of low or minimal harm were selected.
Low or minimal harm was defined as the absence of serious destructive consequences for people or infrastructure; temporary ashfall, short-term disruptions, or minor damage were permitted.

Harm was classified using independent sources describing the consequences of each eruption, including reports from the Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program and the USGS, government communications, and Associated Press reports; a complete list of sources for each event is provided in Supplement S05.
Six eruptions met this criterion:
Holuhraun/Bárðarbunga (Iceland), Anak Krakatau (Indonesia), Fagradalsfjall (Iceland), Mauna Loa (Hawaii, USA), Merapi (Indonesia), and Popocatépetl (Mexico).
These events spanned Europe, Asia, Oceania, and North America.

For this full six-event sample, worldwide search interest in "volcano dream meaning" was higher than expected: for the window comprising the event month and the following month, the mean was 13.33 compared to 7.84 in the seasonality-matched null distribution (p = .03).
Details of the analytical procedure and full results are provided in Supplement S05.
This result is consistent with H5: for a disaster to leave a trace in dreamrelated searches, it need not cause serious actual harm.
Sporting events satisfy many of the conditions previously considered conducive to incorporation and command vastly more conscious interest than disasters.
Yet in dreamrelated searches, their advantage not only disappears but reverses in favor of disasters.
This suggests that current knowledge of the conditions governing the incorporation of content into dreams is incomplete.

This finding also poses a problem for TST: content associated with highly engaging sporting events is weakly represented, whereas both remote disasters and those causing little or no serious harm leave a clear trace in dream-related searches, even though the degree of personal threat is low in these cases.
Both findings are difficult to reconcile with the TST assumption that the intensity of threat simulations should increase with the degree of personal threat experienced in the original situation.

This same pattern, however, is consistent with the predictions of Phantom Anxiety Theory (PAT), which proposes that special priority is given specifically to content involving "safe threats"-objects or events that appear threatening, yet are remote and require no immediate action-rather than simply to content that most strongly engages conscious attention (the continuity hypothesis) or to content associated with a greater degree of personal threat (TST).

If Phantom Anxiety Theory correctly describes the observed pattern of incorporation, this may indicate that the anxiety system has its own information-selection criteria, operating partially independently of conscious goals and interests.
It is possible that some findings supporting the continuity hypothesis in its current form result from a specific measurement artifact.

The idea of continuity between waking-life content and dream content is intuitively compelling, and research participants themselves hold such beliefs (Beaulieu-Prévost et al., 2009; Lambrecht et al., 2013).

text.text: The research procedure itself may therefore distort dream reports through processes of memory selection and reconstruction (Loftus, 2005; Loftus & Palmer, 1974).

text.text: Participants who are consciously and deliberately motivated to report their dreams may "notice" certain contents and associations and regard some as more important or more worthy of reporting, because they believe that "this is what a dream should look like."
The researcher then receives material that has already been filtered through participants' expectations and memory processes and is therefore affected by a self-confirming measurement artifact.
GT-based dream research is free from limitations arising from the research setting itself.
It is therefore possible that when the entire "magic of scientific research" disappears, a pattern of incorporation emerges that differs from what has previously been assumed.

It is also possible that the pattern detected by the present method is difficult to capture using traditional methods and becomes visible only through the analysis of aggregated, spontaneous behavior of millions of users.
The study raises a broader question: Does the mind contain relatively autonomous systems that assign their own priorities to information?
Is the selection of content for incorporation partially governed by such hidden priorities, rather than solely by the intensity of waking attention, emotion, and engagement?
Operationalizing dream content using specific Google Trends queries constitutes a limitation of this study.
Different query formulations may capture slightly different search behaviors; therefore, it cannot be assumed that using other semantically similar phrases would yield identical effect sizes.

The present study does not determine where the observed disparity between sports-related and disaster-related dream content primarily arises-whether during the generation of dream content or during its subsequent recall.
An explanation based solely on differences in the tendency to seek dream interpretation was previously found to be insufficient.
